AI for Social Good
CS 691 · IIT Gandhinagar · Semester II, 2024–25
This course explores how artificial intelligence can address critical challenges in healthcare, education, the environment and public safety, ethically and effectively. It draws on current research at venues such as IJCAI, AAAI, KDD and NeurIPS, and covers both the technical and the societal implications of AI-driven solutions.

Domains
Topics span a wide range of societal domains, including:

  Healthcare: AI for diagnosis, personalised medicine, public health monitoring and remote care
  Environment and sustainability: AI in climate modelling, pollution monitoring, energy efficiency and conservation
  Disaster resilience: AI for disaster prediction, response and resource management
  Education: personalised learning systems, intelligent tutoring and analysis of educational outcomes
  Public safety and security: social engineering, detecting misinformation and predictive policing


Methods
The AI techniques covered include:

  Supervised learning: classification and prediction, such as disease diagnosis, fraud detection and poverty prediction
  Unsupervised learning: clustering and anomaly detection for environmental monitoring and resource allocation
  Semi-supervised learning: working with limited labelled data
  Reinforcement learning: resource optimisation, healthcare interventions and adaptive learning systems
  Natural language processing: sentiment analysis, misinformation detection and speech recognition
  Computer vision: object detection, segmentation and classification for environmental monitoring and healthcare imaging
  Deep learning: neural networks for complex social problems, such as medical imaging and disaster prediction





Questions
How is a paper presentation graded?Each student gives a 20-minute presentation of a paper, graded by the instructor and by peers out of 10 marks: presentation quality (3), Q&A (1), reasons to accept (2), reasons to reject (2) and explaining the approach (2). See Paper presentation.
What are the two paper reviews?Review 1 (5 marks) is done in class and looks at the abstract, the introduction and fatal flaws. Review 2 (15 marks) is done at home on a review platform: everything in Review 1 plus a full AI paper review covering risks, ethics and datasets, informed by existing OpenReview reviews.
What is the project?Groups replicate a NeurIPS-like paper in a social good setting, for 35 marks over three evaluations: a proposal with a Gantt chart, a mid-project progress update and a final presentation. See Paper replication project.
Are guest lectures assessed?Yes. An in-class quiz on the guest lectures is worth 5 marks. The talks are listed on the Guest talks page.
How is class participation counted?One mark for each active class participation, up to 5 marks. Attendance is a separate 5 marks.
Ask anything else on the course Slack.

title: Assessment
text:
Paper replication project
Replicate a NeurIPS-like paper in a social good setting. The project is worth 35 marks over three group evaluations.

EvaluationMarksFormat and criteria

1. Proposal and Gantt chart19 Feb 2025 (Wednesday)10A 10-minute group presentation. Understanding of the paper (4): the paper and its key contributions. Feasibility analysis (3): whether the paper can be replicated with the available code and data. Gantt chart and planning (3): a clear timeline with milestones.
2. Mid-project progressAfter the mid-semester break10A short update presentation of about 10 minutes. Replication progress (5): how much of the paper has been replicated. Challenges and solutions (3): problems faced and how the team is addressing them. Adherence to plan (2): whether the project is on track with the Gantt chart.
3. Final presentationEnd of semester15A detailed group presentation with results and learnings. Successful replication (6): whether the key experiments and results were reproduced. Social good adaptation (5): how well the replication is set in a social impact context. Analysis and insights (4): interpretation of results, limitations and future scope.

title: Guest talks
section: Building infectious disease preparedness and combating AMR using explainable AI
text:
Building infectious disease preparedness and combating AMR using explainable AI
29 January 2025 · Dr. Tavpritesh Sethi, IIIT Delhi · Recording

Abstract
Artificial intelligence (AI) is enhancing clinical decision-making using multimodal data. However, its application has largely been limited to imaging data. In this talk, I will showcase AI’s potential in combating antimicrobial resistance (AMR) and in high-risk intensive care settings. I will discuss barriers such as explainability and evaluation, proposing pathways for AI-enhanced health systems addressing global infectious diseases.


Biosketch
Dr. Tavpritesh Sethi is an Associate Professor at IIIT Delhi and leads the Center of Excellence in Healthcare. With a PhD in computational biology, he is a globally recognised expert in data science for healthcare.
He has received awards for his work in AMR and AI-driven early disease detection from The Trinity Challenge, the Vivli AMR Challenge and MIT Technology Review’s TR35 India. His research focuses on data-driven clinical decision-making, early ICU warning systems and multimodal AI tools. He has published more than 50 papers, is a TEDx speaker, and is a Fellow of the Kavli Foundation and the DBT/Wellcome India Alliance.

title: Guest talks
section: Applying geospatial machine learning for societal impact: Devices, satellites and images
text:
Applying geospatial machine learning for societal impact: Devices, satellites and images
5 February 2025 · Dr. Anupam Sobti, Assistant Professor, Plaksha University

Abstract
As artificial intelligence spreads its wings, it provides us an opportunity to tackle long-standing societal problems by shortening the information gap, whether it is information about the historical produce of a farm to a bank or the declining condition of a road to your local municipal authority. In this talk, I will share examples and opportunities where machine learning based perception systems are being (or could be) used to provide economical and reliable information to the right users at the right time, to address many challenges that arise in these socio-technical systems. We will discuss how these “sentients” could enthuse efficiency in data-driven decision making for policy makers as well as operational pipelines.

title: Guest talks
section: Future of food: Addressing food and water security with machine learning
text:
Future of food: Addressing food and water security with machine learning
20 February 2025 · Alok, Google DeepMind

Abstract
The global food system faces unprecedented challenges. In 2023, 2.4 billion people experienced moderate to severe food insecurity due to climate change and shifting diets. Agriculture contributes significantly to greenhouse gas emissions, necessitating a shift toward sustainable practices.
To feed a projected 9.6 billion people by 2050, the FAO estimates a 60% increase in food production. Machine learning can drive this transformation through digitisation, precision monitoring and data-driven decisions.


Biosketch
Alok is a software engineer at Google DeepMind leading AnthroKrishi, a team focused on remote sensing and AI-driven agriculture solutions. He is a founding member of Climate TRACE and was a Google.org Fellow with WattTime. He has 15 years in technology and leads a 5,000-member grassroots climate group at Google.
